problem_markdown: Colour every point on the boundary of an equilateral triangle with one of two colours. Must there be three same-coloured points forming a right triangle?
solutions_markdown:
Yes. Mark $X,Y,Z$ two-thirds along the directed sides $BC,CA,AB$, respectively. Then $XY\perp BC$, $YZ\perp CA$, and $ZX\perp AB$. Two marked points share a colour; by cyclic relabelling suppose $X,Y$ are red.

If no monochromatic right triangle exists, every point of $BC$ other than $X$ must be blue. Let $W$ be the perpendicular foot of $Z$ on $BC$; it is an interior point distinct from $X$. The points $B,W$ are blue, so $Z$ must be red, or $BWZ$ would be a blue right triangle.

Now $Y,Z$ are red, forcing every point of $CA$ except $Y$ blue. In particular $A,C$ are blue. The midpoint $M$ of $BC$ is also blue, and $AM\perp BC$. Thus $AMC$ is a blue right triangle, a contradiction.
